We’re at a point in the MLB offseason where teams are trying to make as many moves as possible before the sport is set to shut down next week when the owners lock players out.
That rush has led to some big moves like Tarik Skubal signing with the Mets and Trevor Rogers signing with the Orioles, but it’s also led to plenty of smaller moves as team work to build depth.
The Tigers made a move that fell into the latter over the weekend when they signed former Yankees starter Luis Gil to a one-year, $2.3 million deal. It almost immediately got lost in the shuffle when the Mets finished the weekend by signing Skubal to his record-setting deal, but it’s still a fairly big deal given Gil won Rookie of the Year in 2024 and was once viewed as the most important pitcher in the Yankees’ system.
But his time with the Yankees came to an end earlier this month after he was non-tendered, and now he and the Tigers are hoping they’ll be able to partner for a productive 2027 bounce-back campaign.
Sound familiar? It should. The Guardians have made a killing in recent seasons by trading for injured or underperforming starters who had previously had big league success, and the Tigers’ signing of Gil shows they’re trying to do the same thing.
The Tigers are trying to copy the Guardians’ pitching lab success
Gil recorded a 4.61 ERA last year in 27 1/3 innings in a swingman role, marking the second straight subpar season he’s had since winning Rookie of the Year in 2024. Gil finished that Rookie of the Year season with a 3.50 ERA, 171 strikeouts, two complete games and an MLB-leading 77 walks in 151 2/3 innings, which showcased his wild approach combined with his wipeout stuff.
That said, he ended up missing almost all of the 2025 season due to a lat strain before shoulder inflammation wrecked his 2026 campaign. He also missed all of 2023 after undergoing elbow surgery.
That injury led to him pitching out of the bullpen for the first time in his career in 2026, which could provide him with a new avenue for him to help the Tigers. Detroit already has the top of their rotation set with Framber Valdez, Drew Anderson and the recently extended Troy Melton along with having River Ryan, Jackson Jobe and Keider Montero. Gil has more potential than the last three names on that list, but his health is obviously a huge variable.
While the Tigers helped Skubal turn into a two-time Cy Young winner, their pitching pipeline has nowhere near the track record that the Guardians does. We’ll have to wait and see if that’s going to change with Gil.

The New York Yankees spent 2026 making their feelings on Luis Gil abundantly clear, seeking any possible alternative for the rotation while he was healthy and barely giving him a chance to prove his stuff could tick up out of the bullpen down the stretch (it didn't, and his command never came back, either).
Gil's first half in 2024 was the stuff of legends and won him the American League Rookie of the Year award, despite a difficult back half of the season and recovery from (surprise, surprise) injury. Whether it was his release point or a stuff regression in the years that followed (or a combination of the two), he never found consistency again (against any opponent other than the Boston Red Sox, that is, a team he dominated to the tune of an 0.80 ERA in 33 2/3 innings).
Gil's lack of options made him an easy non-tender for the Yankees this winter after he fell out of favor, as well as a difficult bet for any of the league's contenders. He cannot be demoted. He has to be on the MLB roster or the injured list, and it's difficult to find your mechanics when you're in the spotlight constantly.
It seemed like a safe bet that a team that loves the Yankees' pipeline and has enough flexibility to throw darts would be Gil's next destination (the Washington Nationals came to mind). But when reports emerged on Sunday morning that the Red Sox were interested, it was hard not to see the vision. Gil would have no margin for error, but he could recapture his 96 MPH mojo in that particular uniform and become a Brayan Bello type. Of course he could. Of course he would.
But he didn't. It's Gil and the Detroit Tigers, in agreement on a $2.3 million deal that perfectly matches his arbitration estimates.
Where does Luis Gil fit on Detroit Tigers' roster?
The Tigers are known for employing pitching chaos in the postseason, so if Gil survives the entire season on their roster, expect him to be deployed in two-inning sprints throughout October. Last season, Gil was unable to solve the command issues that have long plagued him by attempting to "air it out" in bullpen reps, but he didn't have very long to work on improving his functionality. Maybe the offseason will help.
Gil is probably more Enmanuel De Jesus than he is Troy Melton, at this point, but if he does find a new and workable baseline, we won't be shocked. Thankfully, we don't have to worry about that happening in Boston, and the far more likely reality that Gil is banged-up and largely absent will now play out in the AL Central instead.
Would've preffered the NL, but this is fine.

The Detroit Tigers are reportedly hoping a former American League Rookie of the Year rebounds from an uneven past couple of seasons.
The Tigers and starting pitcher Luis Gil reached a one-year, $2.3 million deal on Sunday, according to ESPN's Jeff Passan.
Two years after Gil won American League Rookie of the Year honors, the New York Yankees declined to tender a contract to the right-hander, making him a free agent.
The decision came before Friday's 5 p.m. ET deadline for offering contracts to players still under club control.
Gil compiled a 3.50 ERA, a 15-7 record and 171 strikeouts in 151 1/3 innings during the 2024 season, looking like a part of the Yankees' starting rotation for years to come.
However, he suffered a high-grade right lat strain during spring training the following season. That sidelined Gil until August. He was effective upon his return, compiling a 3.32 ERA in 11 starts, but his strikeout rate dropped from 10.1 batters per nine innings to 6.5.
This past season, Gil struggled during spring training and was not part of the Yankees' opening day starting rotation.
He joined the major-league roster in April, but registered a 6.05 ERA in four starts (allowing 13 runs in 19 1/3 innings) and was demoted to Triple-A. While with Scranton/Wilkes-Barre, Gil was placed on the injured list with shoulder inflammation and shut down for three months.
Called up just before September, Gil worked out of the bullpen and compiled a 1.13 ERA in five appearances. However, control was a major issue — as it was throughout his Yankees career — with seven walks in eight innings. Ultimately, he was assigned to the Yankees' Florida rookie league affiliate in late September and left off their postseason roster.
Gil, 28, was set for his first year of arbitration eligibility next spring.
The Yankees also non-tendered reliever Fernando Cruz. The 36-year-old right-hander made 61 appearances, striking out 67 batters in 54 2/3 innings. But he sustained a partially torn ulnar collateral ligament in late August, ending his season.
Cruz was acquired before the 2025 season from the Cincinnati Reds in a trade for catcher Jose Trevino. He was one of the Yankees' most effective relievers, notching 72 strikeouts in 48 innings.

Former New York Yankees right-handed starting pitcher and 2024 American League Rookie of the Year Luis Gil agreed to a one-year, $2.3 million contract with the Detroit Tigers, according to Jeff Passan of ESPN.
Gil pitched in five seasons (2021-2022, 2024-2026) for the Yankees. In 56 games (51 starts), Gil went 21-11 with a 3.61 ERA (1.29 WHIP) and 272 strikeouts in 269.1 innings (9.1 K/9 rate).
His best season was 2024, when he went 15-7 with a 3.50 ERA (1.19 WHIP) while striking out 171 batters in 151.2 innings.
Gil debuted in the bigs in 2021, made six starts and showed promise for the future, posting a 3.07 ERA and striking out 38 batters in 29.1 innings.
He began the 2022 season in Triple-A with the Scranton/Wilkes-Barre RailRiders and made one spot start with the Yankees. Unfortunately, Gil struggled on both levels and ultimately underwent Tommy John surgery in May 2022.
Gil was out for the rest of 2022 and all of 2023 minus a pair of starts for Single A-Tampa in the latter season. However, he thrived in 2024, helping the Yankees win their first pennant in 15 years along the way. Gil won all six of his May starts, including a 14-strikeout effort against the Chicago White Sox on May 18.
Unfortunately, Gil didn't get the opportunity to build off his 2024 season momentum. He suffered a high-grade lat strain in March 2025 and didn't make his debut until August. Gil posted a good ERA (3.32) over 11 starts but notably saw his strikeout numbers dip (41 in 57.0 innings) and WHIP rise (1.40).
Gil struggled in 2026. In nine games (four starts), Gil went 1-2 with a 4.61 ERA (1.43 WHIP) with 17 strikeouts in 27.1 innings. He was optioned to Triple-A Scranton/Wilkes Barre on April 26. Unfortunately, Gil dealt with right shoulder inflammation and missed three months last season. The Yankees non-tendered him in November, making Gil a free agent.
Now Gil will get a fresh start now in his second MLB home. Hopefully Gil can finally enjoy a multi-year string of good health, which has unfortunately evaded him in his MLB tenure.

Los New York Yankees decidieron no ofrecerle contrato al lanzador dominicano Luis Gil, quien ahora podrá negociar con cualquier equipo de las Grandes Ligas. La decisión llegó después de dos temporadas complicadas por las lesiones y los problemas de control que impidieron al derecho mantener el nivel que lo llevó a conquistar el premio al Novato del Año de la Liga Americana en 2024.
La salida representa un giro importante para el pitcher de 28 años, que hace apenas dos campañas era considerado una de las piezas más prometedoras de la rotación neoyorquina. Sin embargo, su rendimiento y disponibilidad disminuyeron considerablemente, hasta quedar fuera de los planes contractuales de la organización para 2027.
Gil fue uno de los dos lanzadores no renovados por los Yankees durante la fecha límite para ofrecer contratos, junto con el relevista Fernando Cruz.
De Novato del Año a perder su lugar en Nueva York
La mejor temporada de Gil llegó en 2024, cuando terminó con marca de 15-7, efectividad de 3.50 y 171 ponches en 29 aperturas. Su rendimiento le permitió superar a Colton Cowser en la votación y convertirse en el primer pitcher de los Yankees en ganar el premio al Novato del Año desde Dave Righetti en 1981.
Aquella campaña parecía confirmar que Nueva York había encontrado un abridor con capacidad para mantenerse en la rotación durante varios años. No obstante, las lesiones comenzaron a interrumpir su desarrollo.
En 2025, una distensión de alto grado en el músculo dorsal derecho lo mantuvo fuera del montículo durante los primeros cuatro meses de la temporada. Un año después, la inflamación en el hombro derecho volvió a limitarlo y le costó más de tres meses de actividad.
La campaña 2026 terminó con apenas nueve apariciones en Grandes Ligas, cuatro de ellas como abridor. Gil registró efectividad de 4.61, permitió 21 imparables y concedió 18 bases por bolas en 27 entradas y un tercio, además de sumar 17 ponches.
Los problemas de control marcaron su salida
Más allá de las lesiones, uno de los aspectos que más preocupó a los Yankees fue la pérdida de consistencia en su comando. El dominicano había conseguido destacar por su capacidad para generar swings fallidos y ponches, pero sus dificultades para controlar los lanzamientos terminaron por complicar sus actuaciones.
Durante abril fue enviado a Triple-A Scranton/Wilkes-Barre y posteriormente volvió a la organización de Grandes Ligas, aunque no consiguió recuperar un lugar estable en la rotación.

El gerente general Brian Cashman explicó que la profundidad del cuerpo de lanzadores también influyó en la decisión, pues el equipo llegó a considerar si Gil podía aportar más como relevista que como abridor.
El derecho se encuentra actualmente con los Tigres del Licey en la Liga de Béisbol Profesional de la República Dominicana, donde tiene la oportunidad de continuar trabajando en su recuperación y buscar regularidad antes de la próxima campaña.
Un nuevo comienzo en el mercado de agentes libres
La decisión de los Yankees no significa necesariamente el final de la carrera de Gil como abridor. Su edad, experiencia en Grandes Ligas y los antecedentes de su temporada de 2024 podrían despertar el interés de organizaciones que busquen profundidad para su rotación.
El dominicano tendrá que demostrar que puede recuperar el control de sus lanzamientos y mantenerse saludable durante una temporada completa. Su principal desafío será convencer a un nuevo equipo de que todavía puede acercarse al nivel que mostró cuando se convirtió en uno de los mejores novatos de la Liga Americana.
Después de conquistar uno de los reconocimientos individuales más importantes para un jugador joven, Luis Gil ahora enfrenta una etapa decisiva: encontrar una nueva oportunidad y demostrar que su mejor versión todavía está por venir.

Clarke Schmidt got a contract tender Friday. He didn’t get five innings on the first Saturday in April. That’s the distinction I’d keep in mind as the Yankees put together a rotation that needs five innings at a time from pitchers who can work on schedule.
The same deadline sent Luis Gil into free agency and kept Schmidt and Ryan Weathers on the tendered list, as Bryan Hoch reported. I’d build Schmidt up to start if he’s able. I’d spend the winter as though the Yankees still need someone else to make that first turn.
The Yankees got two different answers in September
He made it back after Tommy John surgery. MLB.com covered his September activation, a milestone that mattered after more than a year off a big league mound. But his official season record shows two outs in one appearance. He struck out both batters he retired. That says very little about how he’d respond after 70 pitches and another start five days later.
The biceps is another part of the decision. The team’s November injury update lists right biceps neuritis and says Schmidt was shut down from throwing in late September. The update expected him to be ready for spring training. A spring training target isn’t a forecast for 25 starts, which is why I’d want a second pitcher prepared to go five while Schmidt builds.
Schmidt’s case for starting isn’t just a distant memory. He spent most of his major league appearances before the injury making starts, and it costs the Yankees less to choose a shorter role in late March after he’s stretched out than to reverse it after he spends camp throwing one inning at a time. If his recovery allows a starter’s program, don’t close off that option in November.
Have someone else ready for that rotation turn
The better test in camp will be the days between outings. If Schmidt puts together a few innings, takes his normal between-start work and then takes the ball on schedule, that’s more useful than how hard he threw on a back field. If he’s fine the day he pitches and keeps needing an extra day after, the workload should tell the Yankees something before an April game does.
Weathers gives New York another name in the mix. The alternative is to build a longer relief role for Schmidt from the first week of camp and spend elsewhere on a starter. I’d choose that if the medical staff wants a shorter progression. Until then, the tender keeps useful upside. Someone else still has to be ready to cover the third time through a lineup in April.

item.content:encoded:
Last night was the last significant date in the offseason calendar before D-Day, which is when the CBA expires on December 1st and the lockout is expected to begin.
In the meantime, teams spent yesterday navigating the non-tender deadline, their last chance to cut ties with players before tendering them contracts for the 2027 season.
For some players who did well early on in their careers, but have since struggled (Jarren Duran is a good example), teams have to weigh the cost of what they are being paid in arbitration with their current production, and sometimes they decide its better to reallocate those resources elsewhere.
You also have players who struggle to stay on the field, putting teams in the position of having to decide if the injury risk is worth the cost.
Today, we are going to dive into the top 5 non-tendered players who I am most intrigued with entering the free agent market. These are guys who I think will be getting an MLB contract, despite just being let go from there’s.
If you are curious who your favorite team non-tendered, at the end of the piece you will find every player who was non-tendered listed by team.
5. Kyle Isbel, Kansas City Royals
Since 2022, there are a total of three outfielders in Major League Baseball that have racked up 50 or more OAA. Pete Crow-Armstrong leads the pack with 64, then Daulton Varsho comes in second with 58, and then you have Kyle Isbel at exactly 50 OAA.
While Isbel provides very little offensively, his glove alone will warrant more big league opportunities, especially in a market that is very thin on center fielders.
4. Luke Raley, Seattle Mariners
This was one of the more surprising non-tenders for me, as I would have thought the Mariners could have traded Raley, even if they didn’t want to have him on their roster for next season. The 32-year-old did not have the best season, but still finished the year with a wRC+ over 100 (106), and 15 home runs.
He is also one of those data darlings who’s quick swing produces plenty of red on his Baseball Savant page. With that said, he also struck out 32.4% of the time last year, whiffed 40.9%, and posted an abysmal 5.2% walk rate.
It’s not crazy that he was cut, but teams also won’t be crazy to give him a guaranteed MLB contract for next season to try recapture the success he had back in 2023 and 2024 (posted a 129 wRC+ each season).
3. Luis Gil, New York Yankees
For Luis Gil to get non-tendered, when he was only projected to make a little over $2 million in arbitration, is a damning statement about his health. Sure, Gil didn’t have any minor league options remaining, but there is a good chance he’d be scooped up if he ever hit waivers anyway.
Two years ago, Gil won the AL Rookie of the Year, posting 29 starts and pitching to a 3.50 ERA for the Yankees in his age-26 season. It looked like he had finally arrived. Unfortunately, right now, he is looking more like a flash in the pan.
Gil has only made 20 appearances since his 2024 campaign, and only 15 of them have been starts. Across the two seasons he has pitched 84 1/3 innings. Gil is currently pitching in Winter Ball, so you’d have to assume he has a clean bill of health at the moment.
The Yankees didn’t think he was worth the risk, but I am sure there are teams with nothing to lose who are going to roll the dice on his upside.
2. Bailey Ober, Minnesota Twins
While Bailey Ober may not have the same recognition as Gil, he provides the thing that teams truly covet more than anything. Innings.
Over the past four seasons, Baily Ober has pitched over 600 innings for the Minnesota Twins, making him on of the 27 starting pitchers in baseball who have completed that feat.
Now to be fair, Ober was far more effective across the first two seasons of that four-year span than the last, but that durability while get him another big league job at the back-end of a thinner rotation.
1. Trevor Larnach, Minnesota Twins
This is the one I just flatly don’t get. Trevor Larnach legitimately had a good season in 2026. In fact, it was a career-year by wRC+ (123) and fWAR (2.2). He hit .269/.352/.436, with 13 home runs and 48 RBIs in 122 games played.
Larnach’s season did end due to a wrist injury that required surgery, but he was still expected to be ready for Spring Training.
For a guy that commands the strike zone so well, takes his walks and making plenty of contact, who is also not a butcher in the corner outfield, it is pretty surprising the Twins couldn’t line up a trade. What they did however line up is some extra room to spend in free agency.
By non-tendering Ober (projected $7.65 million), Larnach ($6.375 million) and by trading Royce Lewis ($5.2 million), the Twins freed up close to $20 million on their books to further allocate in free agency.

The pair were the lone nontenders among the arbitration-eligible Yankees. The club extended contracts to Clarke Schmidt, Luis García Jr., Ryan Weathers, José Caballero, Anthony Volpe, Heliot Ramos and Austin Wells.
It is still possible that Gil and/or Cruz find their ways back to The Bronx, but they now can scan the market after the Yankees declined to extend offers to righties who would have been due around $2-2.5 million through arbitration.
The 28-year-old Gil rose with surprising velocity and dropped when his velocity did, too.
After 2022 Tommy John surgery, he became a star of 2024 spring training and emerged from nowhere to win a spot in the club’s rotation.
With a fastball that lived in the upper 90s, he became one of the most difficult pitchers in baseball to hit (.189 opponents’ batting average), struck out 171 hitters in 151 ⅔ innings and pitched to a 3.50 ERA despite command issues, edging out Baltimore’s Colton Cowser in Rookie of the Year voting.
But he never returned to those heights.
In 2025, he suffered a lat strain in spring training that held him to 11 starts in which he featured lesser stuff. He began last season in the minors, was recalled and pitched to a 6.05 ERA in four games, then was optioned and soon on the injured list with shoulder inflammation.
He returned to the majors in late August as a reliever, and even in the shorter-burst role, his stuff did not meaningfully tick up.
“I think he was finding himself,” GM Brian Cashman said Thursday of Gil’s season. “Essentially, he’s trying to compete in an environment where we are arguably the best, the deepest pitching staff, and so then we got forced into: Is he going to help us more as a reliever versus a starter? Do we need him as a starter? What does it look like out of the pen?”
While Gil’s fall took years, Cruz’s plummet was sharper.
For the majority of his time in pinstripes since arriving in the December 2024 deal that sent José Trevino to the Reds, Cruz was an excellent fireman who entered mid-game danger and typically struck his way out of it. He pitched to a 3.33 ERA with 139 strikeouts in 102 ⅔ innings over the two seasons, numbers that were far better before mid-July.
In his final 16 games of 2026, Cruz pitched to a 5.93 ERA with diminished stuff before he told the club his arm did not feel right. Tests found a partial UCL tear — which often leads to Tommy John surgery that sidelines pitchers for at least a year — but the 36-year-old, wary that he might not make it back to the majors at his advanced age, thus far has chosen to rehab his arm without a procedure. On social media, Cruz uploaded video this week of himself throwing.
“He’s currently rehabbing and I think feeling good and expecting to pitch in 2027,” Cashman said Thursday of Cruz, who had been open about how much he loved and appreciated the Yankees.
A Puerto Rico native, Cruz was drafted as a shortstop in 2007 and did not make his major league debut until 2022. In between, he converted to a pitcher, was released twice, pitched everywhere from the independent New Jersey Jackals to Puerto Rico to Mexico to Venezuela to the Dominican Republic, and discovered a splitter that he calls a “gift from God.”

item.content:encoded:
Why now might be time for Yankees to trade Will Warren and Ryan Weathers originally appeared on The Sporting News. Add The Sporting News as a Preferred Source by clicking here.
The New York Yankees are in a great spot with their MLB roster, especially in the starting rotation. The top of their rotation, led by AL Cy Young winner Cam Schlittler, is as good as any rotation in baseball.
Since the Yankees have such a strong rotation, it would make sense for them to look to ship a player or two out. Will Warren and Ryan Weathers would make the most sense as trade candidates. But should they trade them?
Ken Rosenthal of The Athletic, after Dustin May's $52.5 million contract this offseason, wondered how much value Warren and Weathers hold. With the Yankees' strong rotation and valuable rotation options, now might be the time to sell.
Why Yankees might need to sell Will Warren and Ryan Weathers now
"If $17.5 million per season is the price for such modestly accomplished pitching, then what might the New York Yankees get in a trade for a controllable starter such as right-hander Will Warren or lefty Ryan Weathers?" Rosenthal writes.
This question posed by Rosenthal is one that the Yankees should think long and hard about. The value of Warren and Weathers might not be higher than it is now.
Starting pitchers are a hot commodity right now, especially considering May got such a strong deal despite some shaky performances during his MLB career.
If May is going to get that much money, it would stand to reason that the trade value of Warren and Weathers, two affordable pitchers with a lot of upside, could be through the roof.
Warren is 27 years old and under club control through the 2030 season. He just posted a 3.92 ERA in 2026, better than May's mark this past season.
Weathers is going to be 27 years old on Opening Day 2027 and is under club control through the 2028 season. Last year he posted a 3.60 ERA.
Both of those pitchers are cheap, controllable, and talented. Teams in need of rotation help would surely spend a lot to acquire them.
The Yankees, meanwhile, don't really need either starter. Schlittler, Max Fried, Gerrit Cole, and Carlos Rodon make up the top four of the rotation, with Weathers and Warren options for the fifth spot.
If they trade both Warren and Weathers, they could easily turn to Elmer Rodriguez, Carlos Lagrange, Luis Gil, Chase Hampton, Brendan Beck, or Kyle Carr as their new No. 5 starter.
With great organizational depth and the strong starting pitcher market, now might be the time for the Yankees to trade Warren and Weathers.

item.content:encoded:
As one former AL Rookie of the Year is currently stuck in baseball limbo, the Kansas City Royals could take a bold chance to bolster their depleted pitching staff. New York Yankees pitcher Luis Gil has taken quite a tumble over the past few seasons. He went from one of the best and brightest young pitchers in the game to essentially a throwaway player without a role in New York.
While Gil has recently seen his fair share of struggles, he could become an ideal candidate as a reclamation project for the Royals. The 28-year-old pitcher has thrown just over 84 innings since being named as the top Rookie in the AL in 2024. As a result, he's continued to become buried on the team's depth chart. Now the Yankees will have to make a choice regarding his future very shortly.
According to Joel Sherman of the New York Post, Gil may be non-tendered in November since he is projected to make a little over $2 million in 2027. In an entry into his Pinstripe Post podcast series, Sherman speculated that the Yankees could be willing to part ways with a pitcher that they once held in high regard in order to save that money and spend it elsewhere.
Since Gil will no longer have any minor league options left next season, the Yankees will be very limited in what they can do with him still on the payroll. Thanks to a crowded pitching staff and a number of young arms waiting in the wings, this means that Gil could become expendable for the Bronx Bombers. This creates an interesting opportunity for the Royals.
Luis Gil could give the Royals a dynamic arm on their pitching staff
Unlike the Yankees, who are seemingly blessed with an endless parade of viable arms, the Royals are in desperate need for pitching depth. After a brutal rash of injuries ripped through the pitching staff in Kansas City in 2026, the team struggled to keep their head above water. Those injuries could continue to have a rippling effect well into next season.
Pitchers Cole Ragans, Stephen Kolek, and Luinder Avila all had season-ending surgeries in 2026 and will have a challenging road ahead of them if they are set to return at some point next year. That means that there will be a number of holes to fill throughout the Royals’ pitching staff. Royals GM J.J. Picollo will likely look to free agency to add some affordable arms, but he could look to the Yankees and Gil as another viable option.
Outside of the affordable $2.3 million contract that Gil is set to earn in 2027, he likely wouldn’t cost the Royals a fortune in prospects to acquire either. Without a clear future on the Yankees and limited production over the last two seasons, Gil is now at a diminished trade value that lands squarely inside the Royals’ budget. Even with boom or bust potential, it just might be worth the risk.
In his 20 appearances since 2024, Gil has seen a substantial regression across the board. His walks per nine rate still remains well above 4.5 while his strikeout rate has nearly been slashed in half. Gil has struck out just 58 batters in 84.1 innings of work during that time frame. This was due in part to his lack of control and a drop in velocity over the last two years. Simply put, Gil has no longer been able to get opponents to swing and miss.
Okay, you might read that and think that the Royals would be foolish to even consider dealing for a pitcher who appears to have completely lost his "It" factor. But Gil has dealt with numerous injuries of his own since 2024. From shoulder inflammation to a lat strain, Gil has not been able to stay on the mound long enough to recapture his dominant form. But with a clean bill of health and a full offseason to get back on track, there is optimism that Gil can get back to becoming a successful pitcher in the big leagues.
As a buy-low option for the 2027 season, Gil could be a worthwhile risk for the Royals. If he pitches well enough to help the team get back to postseason contention, he'll be considered a steal. If he pitches poorly and is designated for assignment by June, nobody would blame the Royals' front office for trying. They don't really have much to lose.

A new rumor offers the New York Mets a chance at a young, high-upside starting pitcher in a rare trade with in-city rivals, the New York Yankees.
There is no other way to say it than that the 2026 season for the Mets was one of the worst they’ve had in quite some time. And that is saying something considering their devoted fanbase has seen many underwhelming years. However, there is hope for better days in 2027.
Top star Juan Soto is still in the early stages of his prime. Francisco Lindor had a strong finish to the year. But more than anything, prospects Carson Benge, AJ Ewing, and Nolan McLean showed they have the talent to be key members of a new-look core going forward for President David Stearns to build around.
New York Yankees expected to shop Luis Gil
The Mets will look to upgrade first, second, and third in the offseason, but improving their starting staff will be a far bigger priority. They will surely be linked to superstar free agent Tarik Skubal, but if there is a new salary cap for 2027, the two-time Cy Young may not be a realistic option. That is why Stearns will also need to be crafty and find players that make them better, but who are also cost-effective and under team control for a few years.
Interestingly enough, the Yankees are expected to make a player just like that available soon. According to the New York Post’s Joel Sherman, “The Yankees are going to try like heck to trade Luis Gil.”
The Yankees have a wealth of talent in their starting rotation, and after posting a career- worst 4.61 ERA in nine appearances after dealing with shoulder inflammation, he probably isn’t in their plans to start next season. He could be moved to the bullpen, but that is a big if for the 28-year-old. Furthermore, he is out of minor league options. So they need to come up with a plan or trade him.
What could a Luis Gil trade cost the New York Mets
While Gil struggled last season in limited action and has dealt with injury woes the last two seasons, it can’t be forgotten that he was the American League Rookie of the Year just two years ago. Posting a 15-7 record with a 3.50 ERA and 171 strikeouts to 77 walks. He is also under arbitration control for two more seasons and is expected to make just over $2 million in 2027.
The Yankees don’t have much leverage since Gil’s value is at a low point and they don’t have a clear role for him next season. That could help the Mets in potential trade talks. So what might a deal cost the team from Queens?
The Yankees have a need at catcher after another awful season at the plate for Austin Wells. Would a swap of Gil for Francisco Alvarez interest the Yankees? The Mets may be open to finding a new platoon mate with Gold Glove finalist Luis Torrens. Brett Baty and/or Mark Vientos (along with a prospect) would also be intriguing low-cost options for the team from the Bronx at second or third. Two other positions they will need to address in the winter.
Is a trade likely? Probably not, but Stearns loves a good project. The former ROTY is an affordable option with a ton of upside that he should consider.

item.content:encoded:
We're not quite at the point in the year where the rumor mill is churning in full force, making this current wave of New York Yankees rumors something of an appetizer and a sign that things are going to get much crazier very soon. The looming lockout sets a transaction deadline of December 1, unless the league and the players' union miraculously come to an agreement before then.
That means the month of November is going to be fast and furious. We've already heard about the Yankees' supposed interest in trading for Xavier Edwards, as well as a possible connection to Randy Arozarena. Now, we've got a stack of more fresh rumors to sort through.
Yankees are expected to shop Luis Gil ahead of the November 20 non-tender deadline
It's amazing how far Luis Gil has fallen. The 28-year-old went from 2024 AL Rookie of the Year to a potential centerpiece of a Kyle Tucker trade ahead of the 2025 season to a guy on the roster bubble.
Now, according to Joel Sherman of the New York Post, New York is expected to explore trading Gil before the November 20 non-tender deadline. At this point, he's a reclamation project who, at best, could fetch a change-of-scenery candidate or a lottery-ticket-type prospect or two.
"Keep in mind, Gil and [Clarke Schmidt] are guys, they do not have minor league options left," Sherman explained. "So, they're either on the team next year, or they have to go through waivers. So, if the Yankees feel like they can't help in the rotation, they can't help in the bullpen, there's going to be a thought about either non-tendering or trying to trade one or both."
Sounds like Schmidt is very much in the same boat as Gil, though his recent injury woes might make him even more likely to be non-tendered.
A pair of bullpen arms appear to be in the Yankees' crosshairs on the trade market
After making mostly addition-by-subtraction moves to the bullpen last offseason and failing to address it aside from trading away Camilo Doval at the trade deadline, it sounds like maybe, just maybe, Brian Cashman is going to get serious about revitalizing the relief corps.
On a recent episode of the Pinstripe Post Podcast, Sherman revealed a pair of reliever trade targets that he says the Yankees have liked for a long time, right-handers Jeremiah Estrada and Anthony Bender.
Estrada of the San Diego Padres is a high-octane arm with a big strikeout rate, though he's not without concerns. The 28-year-old hit the IL thrice in 2026, starting with right elbow tendonitis in April, followed by right knee inflammation in June, and finally a right shoulder impingement ended his season early on August 26. His average fastball velocity fell to 95.8 miles per hour this year from 97.9 miles per hour in 2025, and while he struck out 30.2% of batters he faced, he also issued walks at a 12.7% clip.
Marlins reliever Anthony Bender has been someone who has been linked to the Yankees before. He'd also add a much-needed strikeout punch to the 'pen, but in a different way. The 31-year-old is very much an East-West pitcher, with his slider dominating his pitch usage coming in at 65% this year. He pairs that with a sinker that he goes to 32% of the time. Bender's season was impacted for a second straight year with a right shin stress reaction. He tossed 34 1/3 innings in 2026, posting a 2.62 ERA with a 29.3% strikeout rate and an 8.6% walk rate.
It should be noted that Estrada is controllable through the 2029 season, while Bender hits free agency at the end of next season.
Yankees could eye a potential center field platoon partner for Spencer Jones
Lastly, Sherman reported that the Yankees have had past interest in Washington Nationals center fielder Jacob Young, and thinks that they could revisit a trade for the 27-year-old again this offseason to partner with, or even ensure against, Spencer Jones and possible regression.
Young is a glove-first, right-handed hitting outfielder with speed. His bat is very much a work in progress, with him posting a .648 OPS in 2024 and a .583 OPS in 2025 before turning in a career-best .707 performance in 2026. The biggest development in his offensive game has been his ability to hit lefties, slashing .282/.353/.423 against southpaws this year.
It's an interesting fit because, despite being a left-handed hitter, Jones performance against left-handed pitching was one of his biggest strengths. There are questions about his defense, though, and Young would be a nice hedge there. Young also feels like a Yankees kind of player in the Harrison Bader mold.
He has three years of team control remaining, meaning he won't come cheap, especially since his skill set and position could have some viewing him as a starting-caliber player rather than a fourth outfielder. This could make sense, but it all depends on cost.

item.content:encoded:
When one looks at the New York Yankees' roster, the thing that stands out most might be the club's incredible starting pitching depth. Yankees starters led the majors in ERA with a 3.30 mark. Their 3.57 FIP also ranked first, while their 9.43 K/9 checked in at third, and their 2.80 BB/9 came in fifth.
The unit was dominant, and it's even more impressive when you consider that Gerrit Cole wasn't ready to return from Tommy John surgery to begin the season, Max Fried and Carlos Rodón had long chunks of their seasons erased by multiple IL stints, and Ryan Weathers missed the final five weeks of the regular season. The high-end talent was there, but so was the depth, and that will continue into 2027.
| New York Yankees starting pitching depth chart |
|---|
| 1. Cam Schlittler |
| 2. Max Fried |
| 3. Gerrit Cole |
| 4. Carlos Rodón |
| 5. Will Warren |
| 6. Ryan Weathers |
| 7. Elmer Rodriguez |
New York has six starters who would be locks for any rotation in the league. Elmer Rodriguez got his feet wet this year, and while it was a mixed bag for the former top prospect, he'd likely earn a fifth starter job on a good number of clubs thanks to his pedigree and the fact that he didn't embarrass himself when called upon. While they can't be counted on for much given their injury histories, Clarke Schmidt and Luis Gil are still kicking around, for now.
It's an embarrassment of riches, which stands in stark contrast to other areas of the Yankees' roster that need significant overhauls if the franchise is to turn the tide and snap its nearly two-decade-long streak of playoff futility.
At minimum, New York needs a new second baseman and/or third baseman, a catcher, and at least two bullpen arms. A center fielder might be on the docket as well, depending on how you feel about Spencer Jones' ability to hold up defensively. More position player depth is required, and perhaps some additional help in the outfield could be a need, as it's likely that Aaron Judge gets more reps at DH moving forward.
Those are a lot of holes to fill, and in some cases, such as third base, the free-agent market is slim pickings. That brings us to the logical conclusion of trading a starting pitcher for help elsewhere.
The Yankees trading a young, controllable starter isn't the double-edged sword that it seems to be
One can look at everything laid out above and think it's time to pump the brakes on this idea. The Yankees needed to dip down to their seventh starter in Rodriguez six times in 2026, and that number might grow with Fried, Cole, and Rodón all a year older.
That's true, to an extent, but it's also an incomplete picture of the team's needs relative to the market. Last winter, we saw the market for controllable starting pitchers reach unfathomable heights. The Yankees gave up four prospects for Weathers, who up to that point had never thrown more than 94 2/3 innings in a single season.
We also saw an extraordinary deal where five prospects, all in the top 30, moved from the Texas Rangers to the Washington Nationals in exchange for MacKenzie Gore. At that point in time, Gore had just one season with an ERA below 4.00: 2024's 3.90 ERA performance. Then there was the treasure trove of assets the Baltimore Orioles gave up for Shane Baz and the Taylor Ward-for-Grayson Rodriguez swap.
But the one that stands out, and what the Yankees should try to emulate, was the three-team deal that sent Mike Burrows to the Houston Astros and landed Brandon Lowe, Mason Montgomery, and Jake Mangum with the Pittsburgh Pirates.
At the time of that deal, Burrows had thrown just 99 1/3 career innings, and while it was a three-team trade, one can think of this as Houston sending the prospects necessary to acquire Lowe, Montgomery, and Mangum from the Rays, then shipping the trio to the Pirates for Burrows.
Lowe hit 35 homers this season and continued his long resume of stellar play. Montgomery ascended to the closer role and dominated with a 25-inning scoreless streak to end the year. Mangum is a speedy and solid fourth outfielder. Lowe was a one-year rental, but Montgomery and Mangum are under team control through 2030,
Swapping one of Warren, Weathers, or Rodriguez for a similar package that fills three needs would be a huge boost to the team overall, even if it costs valuable starter depth. The market for cost-controlled starters is likely to be just as insane, since what we saw last year was likely a byproduct of the looming lockout.
Starting pitching on the free-agent market is one of the most expensive commodities, so it makes sense that teams would pay big, asset-wise, for less established starters on inexpensive deals.
If the Yankees were able to pull off a trade in which they acquired a position player solution, a reliever, and a bench piece for one of their young arms, they'd still need to replace that depth. They could do so one of two ways.
First, they could re-sign Ryan Yarbrough. The veteran southpaw was only called upon to make two brief starts this season, but in 2025 he proved that he can still be a reliable swingman, making eight starts overall. He'd be cheap and would still be a viable No. 7 starter.
Or, they could go nuclear and sign a top-of-market free-agent starter. Tarik Skubal would be the ultimate prize, but a reunion with Michael King would be almost as intriguing. That might seem like overkill, but if the Yankees want to end the postseason embarrassment, going nuclear might be what it takes.
Trading from their starting pitching depth and taking advantage of an extreme sellers' market is the best way to fill the majority of the roster's holes, making it too obvious a solution for the Yankees to pass up. At the end of the day, this is about asset management and the fact that the No. 6 or No. 7 starter can fetch pieces that will provide much more value than that hurler alone.

7 guaranteed contracts: $210

32 on current 40-man roster plus depth already at AAA

Cam Schlittler (elite with age and stuff upsides)

item.content:encoded:
The 2026 Yankees won 93 games in a year in which superstar Aaron Judge played just 66 games. That’s not a bad total, but it feels like it could, and should, have been more. General manager and Senior VP Brian Cashman routinely builds contending teams, and he should get credit for that, but he and his staff should be aiming higher and doing more to bring the title back to the Bronx.
A Wild Card Series win against the Boston Red Sox was a nice way to start the postseason, but the sweep at the hands of the Tampa Bay Rays exposed many harsh realities that are directly tied to Cashman and his decisions.
For the Yankees, 93 wins is not enough. They need to be the best team in the division, because that would bring them additional benefits in postseason play, such as home-field advantage and a ticket straight to the AL Division Series. Everybody in the organization is responsible for how the season plays out, but the spotlight will always point to the head of baseball operations.
Offseason moves and decisions
Cashman didn’t have a particularly bad offseason, but there were some notable holes when the season started. He didn’t find proper replacements for the rehabbing Anthony Volpe and the underwhelming Ryan McMahon: the former ended up being demoted in early August when the organization promoted George Lombard Jr., and the latter posted a 78 wRC+ and just 0.5 fWAR in 124 games. Volpe eventually returned and played an important role in the stretch run and during the postseason.
Extending Trent Grisham a qualifying offer was seen as a moderate risk when it happened, but it was a reasonable one since the outfielder had hit a career-high 34 homers in 2025. The outfielder declined this year, particularly on defense, but at least it wasn’t a long-term commitment.
The trade for Ryan Weathers was universally acclaimed, and it was a good piece of business on Cashman’s part. He ended up posting career-bests in ERA (3.60), fWAR (2.5), and innings pitched (137.1). The executive also brought back Paul Blackburn, Ryan Yarbrough, Amed Rosario, Paul Goldschmidt, and Cody Bellinger.
Some of them were nice additions, particularly the 2019 NL MVP, but Cashman left the roster exposed to injuries and underperformance in many spots, and that’s on him, too. The bullpen was a bit thin, as some of his past trade experiments, such as Jake Bird, Ángel Chivilli, and Camilo Doval, just didn’t work. The same can be said about Rule 5 pick Cade Winquest. We are more than willing to give Cashman a pass in the bullpen, since the unit finished with the second-best ERA in MLB, though.
Trade Deadline activity (or lack thereof)
The Bombers entered the deadline with a few notable needs, which Cashman was very much aware of. They could have used a catcher given Austin Wells’ season-long slump up to that date, a reliever or two, a starter, and a right-handed outfielder.
They flirted with several backstops, but ended up empty-handed on that front to the frustration of fans. They did bring in Luis García Jr., who had been enjoying an amazing year in Washington with 23 homers and a 133 wRC+.
Heliot Ramos’ arrival was met with mixed reviews, and he posted a disappointing 93 wRC+ in pinstripes. He did have a 184 wRC+ vs. lefties during his time in the Bronx, which was one of the main reasons behind his acquisition. Giving up left-handed pitching prospect Henry Lalane to get him hurt, though. Speaking of…
Prospects and young core
Yes, you could say that the Yankees’ deadline was a disappointment, although some might disagree. However, they managed to keep most of their top prospects, including Lombard, Dax Kilby, Carlos Lagrange, Elmer Rodríguez, and Ben Hess. The promising Lalane was the lone exception.
They represent, together with Cam Schlittler, Ben Rice, Spencer Jones, Weathers, and Will Warren, the next wave of young talent that will, theoretically at least, keep the team highly competitive for the next 3-7 years. Keeping them all, particularly Lombard when half the league was asking for him in trade conversations, was a win for Cashman.
The rest of the farm, however, needs work. A lot of work. The Yankees will need to draft well and be active in the international market in the next couple of years to revamp their depleted system. At least Cashman took a step towards solving the situation, dismissing longtime international scouting director Donny Rowland and replacing him with Mario Garza in January.
Player development wins and losses
As every general manager, Cashman had some player development wins and losses when looking at the final picture of the 2026 campaign. He and his staff managed to turn Blackburn into a very useful reliever with his 1.59 ERA in 85 innings, and he got a nice season from Weathers, too.
Schlittler took a step forward into stardom, and Brent Headrick and Warren also improved in 2026. On the other hand, they couldn’t fix Doval, Luis Gil, McMahon, or Volpe, and Jasson Domínguez remains a fringe player. Grisham and Wells were also subpar for their standard.
The offense, generally speaking, had a mediocre year with a 101 wRC+ that ranked 14th in MLB. Yes, injuries to Judge, Giancarlo Stanton, and other key hitters certainly hurt, but the feeling is that Cashman could have done better, or more.
We have said it multiple times in this space: the Yankees need new voices. They need to listen to more prepared people. They can’t keep doing the same things in personnel decisions, player analysis, research and development, and scouting and expect different results. Unless the ownership decides to part ways with their longtime executive, it will be on Cashman to push that change within the organization: does he have that in him, though? It’s at least a fair question.

item.content:encoded:
The New York Yankees are currently facing the Tampa Bay Rays in the ALDS.
The Yankees will be looking to bounce back against the Rays in Game 2 after losing Game 1. A loss in Game 2 would put the Yankees in an incredibly difficult spot.
Now, as the Yankees continue their series against the Rays, they are now being predicted to trade away two of their pitchers during the offseason.
New York Yankees Predicted to Trade Luis Gil & Ryan Weathers to White Sox
In a recent article for Bleacher Report, Kerry Miller predicted that the Yankees will trade pitchers Luis Gil and Ryan Weathers to the Chicago White Sox this offseason. Miller also predicted that the Yankees will acquire prospects Caleb Bonemer and Pierce George in the move.
“The Yankees also have four more years of Will Warren, two years left on both Luis Gil and Ryan Weathers, one more season of Clarke Schmidt and two MLB-ready 23-year-olds in Elmer Rodríguez and Carlos Lagrange,” Miller wrote. “That’s quite the stockpile of starting pitching that they could use to perhaps pluck a quality prospect from a team that needs to bolster its rotation.”
With the Yankees having plenty of pitchers, it would be understandable if they moved Gil and Weathers this offseason. They need to strengthen their roster elsewhere, while Gil and Weathers could benefit from a fresh start elsewhere.
Looking at Gil & Weathers
Gil appeared in nine games this season with the Yankees, where he had a 1-2 record, a 4.61 ERA, and 17 strikeouts. This was after he had a 4-1 record and a 3.32 ERA in 11 games for the Yankees during the 2025 season.
Gil was memorably named AL Rookie of the Year in 2024 after his strong campaign. In 29 games this regular season for New York, he posted a 15-7 record and a 3.50 ERA. With numbers like these, he could certainly generate interest from a team like the White Sox this offseason.
As for Weathers, he had a 5-8 record, a 3.60 ERA, and 143 strikeouts in 25 games this regular season. Overall, the 6-foot-1 righty had a solid first season with the Yankees. Yet, it is still fair to wonder if he could be moved due to New York’s strong pitching depth.
Bonemer & George Would Be Great Prospects for Yankees to Add
PHILADELPHIA, PENNSYLVANIA – JULY 12: Caleb Bonemer #21 of the Chicago White Sox on the American League Team warms up at Citizens Bank Park on July 12, 2026 in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania. (Photo by Al Bello/Getty Images)
Bonemer would be a very intriguing prospect for the Yankees to add to their system. The 21-year-old just had a monster season in 2026. In 132 games split between High-A and Double-A, he posted 37 home runs, 92 RBI, and a .251 batting average. With numbers like these, he would give New York another exciting prospect who has plenty of power.
As for Pierce, New York would be adding a promising pitcher to their system. The 23-year-old had a 9-3 record, a 3.56 ERA, and 82 strikeouts in 51 minor league games this year.

The New York Yankees enter the offseason with nine arbitration-eligible players projected to cost a combined $36.7 million in 2027, according to MLB Trade Rumors' Matt Swartz, who creates the projections on an annual basis.
But the Yankees could hold on to some of that money by nontendering — that is, declining to offer contracts — to some players.
Two injured pitchers, Clarke Schmidt and Fernando Cruz, are the realistic nontender candidates. Cutting both would trim $6.8 million from the bill.

| Player | Service Time | Projected Salary |
| Clarke Schmidt | 5.148 | $4.5 million |
| Luis García Jr. | 5.142 | $11 million |
| Ryan Weathers | 4.066 | $3.1 million |
| Fernando Cruz | 4.035 | $2.3 million |
| José Caballero | 3.170 | $3.7 million |
| Anthony Volpe | 3.142 | $4 million |
| Luis Gil | 3.119 | $2.3 million |
| Heliot Ramos | 3.103 | $3.2 million |
| Austin Wells | 3.031 | $2.6 million |
| Source: MLB Trade Rumors, "Projected Arbitration Salaries For 2027" — mlbtraderumors.com | | |
Luis García Jr. Tops New York Yankees Arbitration Projections
Luis García Jr. is the lone double-digit case at a projection of $11 million, in his last arbitration year before free agency. He hit .277/.309/.521 with 30 homers and 92 RBI in 147 games between the Nationals and the Yankees, a career year, according to ESPN season statistics.
Anthony Volpe climbs from $3.475 million to a projected $4 million after playing only 70 games. He batted .245/.321/.336 with two homers, 28 RBI and 12 steals, an 88 wRC+ in 234 plate appearances, according to StatMuse's player page for Volpe. The projection reflects his prior platform season and remaining control rather than a full year of work.
He returned in September as a utility infielder after Jazz Chisholm Jr.'s injury and got a look at third base, according to MLB Trade Rumors on Volpe at third.
José Caballero jumps from $2 million to $3.7 million as a Super Two, a designation that allows certain players to enter arbitration a year early — after two years instead of three. Caballero hit .231/.290/.365 with 14 homers and 34 steals in 136 games, fifth in the American League in steals, with an 83 wRC+, according to CBS Sports player page for Caballero.
Ryan Weathers, acquired from the Miami Marlins in January, projects at $3.1 million after 25 starts, 137.1 innings and a 3.60 ERA. He landed on the injured list late in the season with a forearm strain.
Luis Gil lands at $2.3 million, barely above his $2.1625 million salary, after a 4.61 ERA and a 7.13 FIP across 27.1 innings in nine appearances, four of them starts. Heliot Ramos, acquired from the San Francisco Giants at the deadline, is a first-timer projected at $3.2 million after hitting .243/.303/.408 with 13 homers in 112 games, then .198/.309/.379 in 38 games following the trade. Austin Wells, also a first-time arbitration candidate, checks in at $2.6 million with three more years of control.
Fernando Cruz and Clarke Schmidt Face Non-Tender Decisions
Cruz, 36, went on the 60-day injured list in late August with a partial UCL tear and chose rest over surgery, according to CBS Sports. His 3.13 ERA in 54.2 innings came with 67 strikeouts, 32 walks and a 4.18 FIP, walking 5.3 batters per nine innings. Nontendering him saves the full $2.3 million.
Schmidt is projected at $4.5 million, identical to his 2026 salary, after Tommy John surgery in June 2025 and a biceps neuritis shutdown, according to MLB Trade Rumors on Schmidt's injured list placement. The pitcher posted a 3.85 ERA over 323 innings from 2023 to 2025. The projected 2027 staff already lists Fried, Schlittler, Cole, Rodón, Warren, Weathers and Carlos Lagrange, and Schmidt cannot be optioned. Nontendering him saves $4.5 million.
Cruz alone leaves $34.4 million on the books. Schmidt alone leaves $32.2 million. Both exits leave $29.9 million for the other seven.
A pre-deadline deal with either pitcher, the other route for borderline cases, would save less than a full nontender.

item.content:encoded:
With the Yankees one win away from advancing to the ALDS, Aaron Boone wasn’t sure if he would have Aaron Judge for the potential showdown with the Rays.
“Probably too early to tell,” Boone said Wednesday when asked if Judge could return should the Yankees pick up another Wild Card win over the Red Sox.
Judge, recovering from a moderate right calf strain that he suffered on Sept. 16, went to Double-A Somerset to face live pitching on Tuesday. Boone, speaking before Game 2 of the Wild Card Series, wasn’t sure who threw to Judge. The manager said the potential options included Luis Gil, Eli Morgan and Justin Topa.
Boone also wasn’t sure what, if any, running Judge did on Wednesday. On Tuesday, the skipper said that Judge would have to run the bases before he could be “a full player” for the Yankees.
On Wednesday, Boone also didn’t rule out the idea that the Rays’ home could impact whether the Yankees roster Judge for the ALDS. Tropicana Field has a turf field, the type of surface that isn’t kind to lower-body and leg injuries. Even when Judge is healthy, Boone tries to get him a DH day or two at The Trop when possible.
“I guess that could [make an impact],” Boone said, “but we’ll see where we are in hopefully making that decision in a couple days.”
In addition to baserunning — Judge did do some light running and agility work in the outfield at Yankee Stadium on Tuesday — the back-to-back MVP still needs to do defensive work. Judge did face live pitching during Monday’s pre-postseason workout, too.
“He had to check a lot of boxes for the trainers and the strength guys to say, ‘OK, you’re ready for that, you can go do that,’” Boone said. “I feel like in the couple weeks since the injury, he’s made real strides and significant improvements. Hopefully, we’re in a position to make another decision in a couple of days.”
Aside from Judge’s rehab plans, Boone also addressed the slugger’s absence from pregame introductions on Tuesday. Judge’s name noticeably wasn’t called as the Yankees took to the first base line — others left off the Wild Card roster participated — but Boone indicated he was getting treatment.
“I didn’t even know until it happened,” Boone said. “But I think a couple of the injured guys weren’t involved in it. But I think he was getting treatment stuff.”

item.content:encoded:
New York Yankees general manager Brian Cashman spent the 2026 trade deadline adding offense. With Aaron Judge still out and Giancarlo Stanton permanently MIA, it made some sense on paper to add bats like Luis García Jr. and Heliot Ramos.
You know what didn't make sense? Walking away from the deadline without a single pitching addition. And yet, that's exactly what Cashman did. For whatever reason, Cashman deemed that the market wasn't right to add reliever depth, despite the fact that the Yankees have been running arms like Brent Headrick and Fernando Cruz into the ground all season long.
Not surprisingly, Headrick is beginning to show signs of fatigue (he is human, after all), and Cruz is now injured. The Yankees are signing no-name arms to stay afloat, and Cashman deserves blame for this situation. At least New York Post's Joel Sherman is seeing things clearly.
Brian Cashman thought he could get away with Yankees current bullpen
Are Yankees really still hoping that arms like the untrustworthy Luis Gil or the recovering Clarke Schmidt will help make this crisis go away? That's where we're at entering October, and it's sad.
This roster has a ton of talent, and the American League is decidedly weak this season. But since Cashman ignored the pitching staff at the deadline, their World Series chances have no doubt taken a hit.
While the overachieving Tampa Bay Rays held off the Yankees and Red Sox, and New York deserves credit for emerging from the "grave danger zone" of losing ground to Boston, this front office oversight still doomed them to the Wild Card. Cruz's injury alone doesn't prove this, by the way — he'd been awful since the All-Star break. Anyone watching the Yankees has been able to see that their bullpen has slowly been breaking down. It was happening way before the deadline! It's a miracle things aren't much worse.
Fans can't be too shocked at Cashman's performance (or lack thereof). This has become an annual tradition. He makes false assumptions that the Yankees have enough depth in a certain area (oftentimes the pitching staff), and they never do. He hates purchasing insurance, despite evidence to the contrary that this team underachieves in August (almost every year) and enters the playoffs wounded and tired.
Getting to the postseason has never been a problem for the Yankees during the Cashman era. It's the whole advancing once they get there that's been consistently disappointing, and you can trace that back to Cashman's deadline every season.
Max Fried came back earlier than expected. Great! Schmidt vacillated between being close and injured. Splendid! None of that changes the fact that Cashman should have added reinforcements at the deadline and failed to do so. The script is so familiar at this point. Fans just want something different for once.

With the New York Yankees locked into an American League Wild Card berth, anticipation is building around who will make the final postseason roster—especially after former AL Rookie of the Year Luis Gil was optioned to the Florida Complex League ahead of October.
Gil was optioned alongside fellow right-hander Bradley Hanner, leaving one final roster spot up for grabs, as the Yankees announced on Thursday. While Gil had an opportunity to pitch his way onto the October roster, a rocky, walk-heavy outing against the Tampa Bay Rays sealed his fate.
In addition to bullpen decisions, the Yankees are closely monitoring their key injured stars as October approaches. On that front, manager Aaron Boone addressed the media to clear the air regarding conflicting reports about Aaron Judge’s status.
Boone also remains hopeful that slugger Giancarlo Stanton can return in time for the postseason, as the organization continues evaluating his physical readiness through live drills and simulated games.
Luis Gil #81 of the New York Yankees throws a pitch.
Yankees’ potential postseason roster
While the front office awaits definitive health updates on Judge, Stanton, and outfielder Trent Grisham, the baseline roster is coming into focus for their Wild Card showdown against the archrival Boston Red Sox, who are facing injury concerns of their own regarding catcher Willson Contreras.
Here is how the Yankees’ postseason roster is projecting:
- Starting Rotation: Gerrit Cole, Max Fried, Carlos Rodón, Cam Schlittler, Will Warren
- Relief Pitchers: David Bednar, Paul Blackburn, Michael Fulmer, Brent Headrick, Tim Hill, John Schreiber, Ryan Yarbrough
- Catchers: Austin Wells, Ali Sánchez
- Infielders: Jazz Chisholm Jr., Paul Goldschmidt, Ryan McMahon, Anthony Volpe, José Caballero, Luis García Jr., Amed Rosario, George Lombard Jr., Ben Rice (1B/DH)
- Outfielders: Cody Bellinger, Heliot Ramos, Spencer Jones
As New York prepares for October baseball, fans are eager to watch the latest chapter in the game’s greatest rivalry unfold, with a spot in the ALDS against the division-champion Tampa Bay Rays hanging in the balance.

A chaotic final 72 hours of the Yankees' regular season will begin with a last-minute doubleheader on Friday, combining two weekend affairs against the Baltimore Orioles into one evening. Requiring some pitching help for the doubled-up games, the Yankees demoted both Bradley Hanner and Luis Gil after Thursday's exciting win.
Could this mean Carlos Lagrange's MLB debut, after Matt Blake hinted that he wasn't elevated on Friday because of the timing of his live BP? Everyone believed ... right up until their hopes were dashed four hours before gametime.
Instead, the Yankees will elevate Brendan Beck and Yerry de los Santos, and Lagrange, always a playoff longshot, now feels like an impossibility.
The Yankees enter Friday needing to turn the emotional tide after a weather shuffle that's left some fans feeling short-changed. After all, CC Sabathia's big day and Monument Park ceremony were set for Saturday before the rains necessitated a change of plans, and not everyone is happy with the last-minute alteration. Sabathia even reacted to the broken hearts on his own social media account.
Yankees must change the vibes after last-second alteration to CC Sabathia ceremony
Holding Sabathia's Monument Park ceremony on the final weekend of the season - as well as a Josh Hart bobblehead giveway that's sure to cause riots and also got partially scuttled - was a choice meant to import massive crowds for an AL East showdown the Yankees surely hoped would matter. It won't, and for a totally fine reason - the Yankees fell short of the division crown, but left the rest of the league in their wake, and are totally locked in.
Fans holding the Yankees accountable for changes in the weather are being unreasonable. It's also difficult to expect them to tell Sabathia, at the very last minute, to go home and prepare himself again for a do-over next season. But ... that doesn't mean this doesn't suck. It sucks for fans with Saturday tickets who are unable to use them on Friday - the Yankees probably should've at least figured out a way to make this a double-admission doubleheader and do the Sabathia game and bobblehead together for the late game. And it also sucks for Sabathia, who was due a full house in primetime and will instead get a Nor'Easter-beating daytime crowd at 3:15 PM EST.
At least the fans who got the short end of the stick have received an electric gift of ... Brendan Beck to perk up this final meaningless series. Oh, well.

(Photo credit: Brad Penner)
Rookie George Lombard Jr. hit an impressive tiebreaking two-run homer with two outs in the eighth inning as the New York Yankees overcame a four-run deficit and earned a 6-4 victory over the Tampa Bay Rays on Thursday night.
The Yankees (92-67) won for the 11th time in 16 games thanks to their late comeback that was sparked by Lombard.
Following a single by Amed Rosario off Steven Matz (5-6), Lombard snapped a 4-4 tie by lifting a 2-2 sinker into the second deck of the left field seats. It was Lombard's seventh homer in 41 games since joining the Yankees last month and his fourth in the past seven games.
Lombard also hit an RBI double during New York's three-run seventh and scored on a wild pitch to the backstop by Tampa Bay rookie Brody Hopkins.
Paul Goldschmidt had a tying RBI single in the seventh for the Yankees, who are 11-8 when tied through seven innings.
Austin Wells also homered for the Yankees, who had one hit through the first five innings and lost seven of 13 meetings with the top-seeded Rays (96-63).
New York ace Cam Schlittler allowed two runs (one earned) on three hits in three innings as he was limited to 70 pitches in his final start before the postseason. The right-hander struck out five and finished with 239 strikeouts to go along with a 1.95 ERA in his first full season.
Bradley Hanner (1-0) retired Junior Caminero to end the eighth and stranded a runner in the ninth for his first career victory.
Caminero had an RBI single and a run-scoring double as the Rays held a 4-0 lead into the sixth. Caminero needs one RBI to become the fifth player in team history with multiple 100-RBI seasons.
Yandy Diaz added a pair of hits, including a hit that scored a run on a throwing error by New York right fielder Heliot Ramos in the third.
Caminero gave the Rays a 2-0 lead with a single to center field and followed with a double off the left field fence before Tampa Bay took a 4-0 lead on an error by reliever Luis Gil.
Tampa Bay's Ian Seymour allowed one hit in five innings. He struck out three and walked none in a 58-pitch outing.

The New York Yankees optioned Luis Gil to the Florida Complex League on Thursday night, pairing the move with the demotion of fellow right-hander Bradley Hanner ahead of a weather-compressed series against the Baltimore Orioles.
The announcement itself was terse. The story behind it is not.
Two seasons after Gil won American League Rookie of the Year, the 28-year-old has become a cautionary tale of how quickly a breakout can fade.
In 2024, he looked like a rotation piece the Yankees could build around: 15-7 with a 3.50 ERA, 171 strikeouts in 151⅔ innings, and a fastball that still touched the upper 90s. He was not a fluke filler. He pitched like someone who belonged in the middle of a contending staff.
What followed has been a slow unraveling. A high-grade lat strain wiped out most of 2025. When he returned in August of that year, he posted a respectable 3.32 ERA in 11 starts, but the underlying numbers told a different story.
Strikeout rate cratered. Walks climbed. Velocity dipped. The same four-seamer that once generated swings and misses suddenly looked hittable. The 2025 cameo was a mirage dressed up as a win-loss record.
2026 has been worse. Gil opened the year in Triple-A, earned a brief rotation look in April, and promptly allowed six runs in four innings against Houston. The Yankees sent him back down.
A later shoulder issue further interrupted his season. Recalled in late August, he was used almost exclusively in low-leverage relief.
The results were mixed at best: occasional clean innings mixed with walks and a homer problem that never fully disappeared. His 2026 line through Thursday sat at 1-2 with a 4.61 ERA in 27⅓ innings, a far cry from the pitcher who once looked like a mid-rotation lock.
Sending a former Rookie of the Year to the complex league is not a routine roster shuffle. It is a statement that the organization no longer sees him as a major-league contributor in the immediate term.
Whether this is a last-ditch reset, a roster crunch created by returning arms, or simply an admission that the command and stuff have not returned, the optics are grim. Gil still has years of team control remaining.
That fact only makes the disappointment sharper. The Yankees once believed they had found something special.
Two years later they are shipping him to the lowest level of the system before a series that should have been about playoff positioning, not roster housekeeping.
The 2024 version of Luis Gil feels like a different pitcher. The current one is still searching for him.

item.content:encoded:
The New York Yankees have three main arms in their bullpen who they can rely on during the postseason. This trio of relievers consists of closer David Bednar, Brent Headrick and Paul Blackburn, the Yankees' best relief assets all season.
But who can they count on in the trust tree behind these three relief pitchers? Let's try to project which bullpen arms the Yankees can lean on in the playoffs from most to least trustworthy.
Yankees' most trustworthy relievers as playoffs approach
Yankees manager Aaron Boone has Bednar, Headrick and Blackburn, who he can go to in the late innings if the team has the lead or is in a tie game. But the Yankees are going to need more than that if they're going to make a deep run.
This is where Will Warren will likely come in as someone that can give the Yankees some key innings in long relief in the playoffs. Warren has not allowed a run in three innings as a reliever this season, and has pitched well as of late overall (2.45 ERA in September).
Hear me out on this next one: If Tim Hill makes the postseason roster, he will step up for the Yankees. Hill has allowed just one earned run across 11.1 playoff innings for the Yankees in the last two years. Since May 31, Hill has seen his ERA balloon from 2.53 to 4.71. But he is postseason tested, which means Boone and the Yankees should be able to count on him.
Last but not least, the sixth most trustworthy bullpen option could be newcomer John Schreiber. The right-hander has a 2.00 ERA over nine innings since joining the Yankees at the beginning of the month. Like Hill, Schreiber has postseason success, posting five scoreless relief appearances against the Yankees, ironically, in the 2024 postseason while pitching for the Kansas City Royals.
Who the Yankees shouldn't trust in ther playoff bullpen
Now we get to the part, where the names on this list probably should be pitching in lower leverage spots in the postseason. Fernando Cruz would've been included here, but his return is in doubt due to a partially torn UCL in his right elbow. Beyond Cruz, there is a pair of starters who are coming back from injury that likely can't be trusted at this point.
No. 1 is Clarke Schmidt, who just experienced biceps soreness when trying to warm up in the bullpen on Sunday. Schmidt came back from 2025 Tommy John surgery on September 16, but has been limited to one appearance, where he recorded two outs. It's hard to see how he could be high up on the trust tree in the postseason if the Yankees keep him on the playoff roster.
The second starter is Ryan Weathers, who had a breakout season for the Yankees this year. The expectation was that Weathers could be a solid relief option in the playoffs, but he is now unlikely to return in the regular season due to his left forearm flexor strain. It's difficult to envision Weathers coming back healthy at this point and being a trusted reliever in the biggest games of the year.
Should the Yankees choose to go: Cam Schlittler, Max Fried, Gerrit Cole, Carlos Rodón, Bednar, Headrick, Blackburn, Warren, Hill, Schreiber, Weathers, Schmidt, that would mean there's one more spot available for a pitcher on a 13-man staff. This last slot would come down to: Luis Gil, Michael Fulmer or Ryan Yarbrough.
While Gil has the most upside of the three, he can be erratic with his command at times. He also has a 6.75 ERA for his career in the postseason. Fulmer has a 4.50 ERA since joining the Yankees last month and Yarbrough is better suited to give length when the team is trailing. Whoever the Yankees decide to give the last spot to will be a low leverage option and at the bottom of the trust tree.

Updated Yankees projected Wild Card Series roster without Aaron Judge
NEW YORK - Here was the scenario these Yankees hoped to avoid, but couldn't - a triumphant Tampa Bay Rays team, celebrating their AL East title on Bronx turf.
"They've put together a fantastic regular season to earn that,'' said manager Aaron Boone, after the Rays' 6-1 victory in Tuesday's nightcap of a split doubleheader at Yankee Stadium.
"Hopefully, we get another crack at them.''
That would be in a best-of-five AL Division Series, but only if the Yankees advance from a best-of-three Wild Card series, which they'll host - likely against the rival Red Sox.
With that Wild Card opponent in mind, here is our updated version of a Yankees 26-man playoff roster (12 pitchers, 14 position players), for a series that would begin on Tuesday, Sept. 29.
Rosters can be altered before each postseason round. Injured players can be replaced in-series (pitcher for pitcher, position player for position player) but the injured player is ineligible for the next playoff series.
Projected Yankees pitchers (12)
Starters (3): RHPs Cam Schlittler, Gerrit Cole; LHP Max Fried.
Relievers (9): RHPs David Bednar, Paul Blackburn, Will Warren, Michael Fulmer, John Schreiber; LHPs Ryan Weathers, Tim Hill, Brent Headrick, Carlos Rodon.
On the bubble: RHPs Clarke Schmidt.
Also available: RHPs Luis Gil, Elmer Rodriguez, Yerry de los Santos, Bradley Hanner, Carlos Lagrange; LHP Ryan Yarbrough.
Currently injured: RHPs Fernando Cruz, Angel Chivilli, Kervin Castro.
Analysis: Would the Yanks start anyone but Schlittler in Game 1?
Well, nothing's been firmly stated about the first round rotation, though Schlittler - the odds-on choice for the AL Cy Young Award - would be on normal rest for the opener.
Cole (Wednesday) and Schlittler (Thursday) will make their final regular season starts during this Rays series, though Boone mentioned limiting both starters in these tune-ups for postseason.
In the bullpen, Schmidt's recent bout of biceps cramping wasn't fully resolved as of Tuesday; he was due to be re-examined after a throwing session.
It's possible that even a slight setback takes Schmidt out of consideration for an important playoff spot, moving Michael Fulmer off the bubble and on the roster.
Rodon's eight shutout innings in Tuesday's doubleheader opener was his best effort, during an impressive stretch drive.
He'd be certain to start Game 1 or 2 of a Division Series vs. the Rays, but the Yanks might need his services - in some capacity - to advance vs. Boston, so he's now included here.
Projected Yankees infielders, utility/DH (9)
Infielders (7): Luis Garcia Jr., 1B; Paul Goldschmidt, 1B; Ben Rice, 1B-DH; Jazz Chisholm Jr., 2B; George Lombard Jr., SS; Anthony Volpe, 2B-SS; Ryan McMahon, 3B.
Utility players: (2): Jose Caballero, IF-OF; Amed Rosario, 3B-2B.
On the bubble: None.
Also available: Max Schuemann.
Analysis: Garcia and McMahon are slumping at the wrong time, while Chisholm - who just returned off the IL (right thumb sprain) on Tuesday - has this week to find his rhythm again at the plate.
But that trio of lefty hitters might all be starting on the bench against Boston, which could employ three lefty starters against the Yanks.
That puts Caballero in play as a third base option, with the veteran Goldschmidt (.997 OPS vs. lefties) at first base, the rookie Lombard at short, and Volpe recast as a second baseman.
Projected Yankees outfielders (3)
Cody Bellinger, Spencer Jones, Heliot Ramos.
On the bubble: None.
Also available: Jasson Dominguez.
Currently injured: Aaron Judge, Trent Grisham.
Analysis: That's a thin outfield without Judge, whom the Yanks are not planning to have for at least the Wild Card series - per Boone - due to the captain's "moderate'' right calf strain.
It's increasingly unlikely that Grisham (strained hamstring) is available, too, by next week, and that presents a danger considering Ramos' defensive deficiencies.
For that same reason, Dominguez is on the outside. Mostly, the Yanks need the potent right-handed bats of Ramos (who has found his hitting groove) and Rosario to combat Boston's lefty pitching.
Caballero could find himself pressed into outfield duty, too.
Without Judge, "it's going to be super tough on us,'' said Ramos. "But we're going to go forward, for sure.''
Yankees' projected catchers (2)
Austin Wells, Ali Sanchez.
On the bubble: None.
Also available: J.C. Escarra.
Analysis: Wells has been a better offensive presence after a brutal first half, and Sanchez has learned the staff and he earned much praise from Rodon for his contribution to Tuesday's game one win.
Boone has kept the Cole-Wells pairing together, and you'd still anticipate Wells getting starts vs. Boston's lefty starters throughout this opening series.
